title: Briefs
goal: What a brief is, how an outline is picked from the candidates, hand-pinned overrides, and the rules that keep a brief faithful.

blocks.x: What a brief is

A **brief** is a word's outline taken from Plover's or Lapwing's gold dictionary instead of derived from lyk's phonetic rules: [[he|E]], not `HAOE`. A brief may be a memorized shortcut with no phonetic link to its word. A word's primary outline from any source need only be the **cheapest** available, not guessable.
`rules/briefs.toml` sets the default source (`plover`), how many of the most common words get a brief (`count = 1500`), and the per-word overrides.
How a word's outline is picked
Every word's primary outline is settled by **one global optimization**, not sequential passes. Candidates for every word:

items: both gold dictionaries' listed outlines (the briefs),
a spelling-distinguished variant for a homophone group,
the full star ladder on all of the above,
for a word spelled with a trailing `s`, a voiced `-Z` coda respelled `-S` on any of the above that has one.

blocks.x: The solver picks the assignment minimizing the **whole dictionary's total cost, weighted by word frequency**. A brief, a rules-derived reading and a brevity-shortened form compete in one pool for the word; the cheapest wins, weighed against other words' stakes in the same strokes. A brief is not pinned when found.
The solver and its inputs are described in [How the solver works](#/ref/how-solver) and [Candidates, cost and ergonomics](#/ref/how-candidates-cost).
Cost: strokes, then keys, then comfort
Candidates are ranked by one function everywhere:
cost = 25 000 per stroke + 1 000 per key + ergonomics (always under 1 000)

items: A stroke costs more than all the keys one stroke can hold (24): for a single word **fewer strokes always wins**.

Tied on both: the **more comfortable** outline wins, possibly a starred outline over a star-free one if easier to press (Plover lists both `PW*ES` and [[best|PWEFT]] for *best*; the cost model settles it).

A **family-shaped** candidate (a word's root outline plus its ending's key, see [Syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables)) counts two keys cheaper than it is, so a family shares one shape unless that costs more than two extra keys.

blocks.x: A stroke weighs 25 keys: [[like|HRAOEU]] beats `HRAOEUB`, [[day|AEU]] beats `TAEU`; *you* stays [[U]], not 7-key `KWRAOU`.
Frequency decides who gets a contested stroke

Frequency never changes a candidate's own cost: two words considering one outline agree on its cost. Who gets it depends on each word's total result, using the **raw usage count** in the frequency corpus. The solver's objective is exactly the headline number `!build` and `!score` report: average keys per word, weighted by frequency.
Losing a stroke is the normal mechanism

A word that loses a contested outline to a more valuable word is not a failure. Every word keeps a full ladder of fallbacks (plain reading, star on the first stroke, star on the last, then one and two extra star strokes) as real candidates, so losing never forces a long phonetic spelling-out while a cheap ladder step is free. See [When two words sound the same](#/ref/collisions).

A guard counts words whose final outline costs more than their own plain-rules reading although that reading is unclaimed (family-shaped words exempt). `!build` prints it as "words stranded on a worse outline than their own, unclaimed plain reading"; a test holds it to zero, as a true global optimum cannot leave a cheaper free outline unused.
When a cluster has too few strokes

When more mutually exclusive words want a set of strokes than there are legal outlines (a homophone or near-homophone cluster tighter than its star ladder), the solver **sacrifices the word with the least to lose**. Every word's pool includes a private "no match" option priced at the cost of no outline: the word is **fingerspelled**, one stroke per letter, never less than one stroke worse than its worst real candidate, scaled by frequency weight.

A rare name losing its last slot is weighed against a common word's extra stroke. Example: *early*, said about 85,000 times, keeps [[early|ERL]]; the rarest of its cluster (*errol*, *earle*, *earl*) pays. `!build` counts words left unplaced this way as "words the rules could not place"; every one is rarer than rank 20,000.
A brief may not drop a sound for free

A gold outline missing a key of the word's first onset (*grab* `RAB`, *graph* `TPWRAF`, *got* `TKPOT`) is offered only if it saves a whole stroke on every other candidate, the word is among the 550 commonest, or it is pinned in `rules/briefs.toml`. The end of the word is free: [[find|TPAOEUD]] drops the N. Rule, allowances and the measured 550: [faithful outlines](#/ref/collisions). A pinned `plover` or `lapwing` source counts as pinned; *got* and *find* are pinned to their faithful outlines.
Extra one-stroke entries

After everything else is placed, a word's other one-stroke candidates that lost the primary slot take any still-unclaimed stroke. Candidates: gold briefs from Plover and Lapwing that key the first onset (see [faithful outlines](#/ref/collisions)); briefs from other theories that save a stroke (see [other theories' briefs](#/ref/collisions)); the other theories' faithful, typable one-stroke briefs that do not save one; the plain rules reading; a spelling variant; an `-S` respelling; a family shape.

items: **At most three per word**, cheapest first, each **within three keys** of the word's own outline.
Star and `/+*` ladder markers are collision fallbacks: excluded.

They run strictly last: they never take a stroke any primary, backup or phrase wanted, and every lookup tool ranks them below the primary. *like* is [[like|HRAOEU]] with other one-stroke outlines as extras.

**Kept from rare words.** A word said at most 200 times that holds the stroke of one of another word's four cheapest extra options, that word being at least 30 times as common, gives the stroke up and the common word gets it as an extra, before short forms and phrases (see [a rare word does not hold a common word's extra](#/ref/collisions)). *ease* has [[ease|AOEZ]] beside [[ease|AEZ]]; the junk *ees* does not.
The current build has about 33,000 of them.

blocks.x: Hand-pinned overrides

In `[word]`, a source of `"plover"` or `"lapwing"` only narrows which gold dictionary supplies brief candidates; the word still competes on cost. A **literal outline** is a human choice for that word, never reopened against the word's other candidates or another word's.

items: A literal override resolves first, like a reserved outline or standalone suffix, so every other word's candidate pool treats the stroke as taken from the start.

A collision between a literal override and something already pinned (reserved stroke, suffix table, *I*, another override) is a **hard build error** to fix in `rules/briefs.toml`, never silently resolved.

blocks.x: The single-key words

The join key doubles every continuation shape into a separate outline (`+-G` is *ing*; a bare `-G` is not that stroke), so a single right-hand key is free for a whole word. Of the ten single right-hand keys, six are claimed here; the others are [[of|-F]], [[be|-B]], [[the|-T]] and [[for|-R]].
*were* does not get [[-R]]: *for* is commoner and keeps it; *were* is [[were|WR]] (W, then the reduced vowel's R).

Short briefs for very common words

Exception to "derivable from sound": for sufficiently common words a memorized stroke beats five or seven reconstructed keys. Each was checked against the candidate pool and real collisions before pinning.
The th family is pinned

Every word beginning with the "th" sound of *they* is written with `TH-`, the vowel distinguishing them, so knowing one gives the rest. Pinned because the solver, left alone, chose the shortest chord for each (`-BLS` for *their*, `-FBL` for *those*, `-RPG` for *these*): a key saved, with nothing in the chord indicating the word.
The same family, not pinned but following the pattern: [[this|TH]], [[them|THEP]], [[there|THR]].
No half-held key combinations

A candidate may not take only **part** of a key combination the rules use only **together** for one sound. Applies to every raw gold-dictionary candidate. Example: Plover's `KPWAOD` for *good* keeps the `P W` of `TKPW` (the rules' "g") but drops the `T`, reading back as "k", not "g": a different sound. *good* is [[good|AOD]].

A raw candidate failing the check is never offered. Up to two **repairs** are generated from it and offered as separate candidates: completing the fragment into the whole cluster, or dropping it. A brief may skip a sound, so dropping is usually fewer keys and tends to win when both are legal. A repair exists only because the gold dictionary pointed at that sound.

A sound explains a key only if it can sit on the stroke being checked: every syllable for a one-stroke brief; for a multi-stroke outline, only the first `syllables - strokes + 1` syllables for the first stroke and the last that many for the last (every other stroke holds at least one syllable). Otherwise the second stroke's "t" of *dictate* would explain the first stroke's `TK` ("d"), and the lone `K` would be "repaired" into `TEUBG/+TAEUT`.

A literal override is exempt from this check (a human chose it) and from the faithful check above, so a literal override should not be a half-held chord. Six old overrides (*on*, *from*, *no*, *then*, *day*, *which*) exploited an older, narrower check and were removed; each word takes its own full phonetic reading. (*which* was later pinned to [[KH]] for another reason, listed above.)
`W` is never a stand-in for `V`

Plover and the other theories write some `v` with the left-hand `W` key (`TKWAOEUD` for *divide*, `KWERT` for *convert*). lyk's `V` is `SR`, and `W` is only the `w` sound or a key inside another chord (`PW` b, `TKPW` g, `KWR` y). A gold brief whose left-hand `W` is none of those (the word has a `V`, and no `W`, `B`, `G`, `Z`, `ZH`, `JH` or `Y` sound) is not offered as listed: its `W` is rewritten to `SR` and the result competes like any other brief, so it is never an outline you could not derive from the sounds.

*divide* is [[divide|STKRAOEUD]] (`TK` d plus `SR` v), *divine* [[divine|STKRAOEU]], *convert* [[convert|SKRERT]]. The rewritten stroke is settled like any other outline: where it lands on a stroke another word already holds, that word keeps it and the other falls to its next outline.
